title: Jingles he refused and writing with restrictions
summary: A few jingles he could not put his name on; writing for singers is easy, while total freedom is hardest.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I see. Behind the scenes. Fascinating. Did you ever get a call to do a jingle that you just said I can’t do this.
Yeah. A couple. I won’t elaborate, but there were a couple I just couldn’t put my name on. I couldn’t put my soul into it, no.
Did you ever get one that you said I can’t do this and then your musical mind started working despite yourself?

I might have. I really can’t remember. It might have but it’s possible. I’ve had that happen with singers when I arrange for singers or not arrange for singers and after the fact I’d say you know I could have done this, I could have done that. But really, for singers, they’re a different breed. But that’s easy work because the melody is covered. All you have to do is just support that singer. Yeah, the easiest writing you’ll ever get in your life is when the producer or the director or whoever says, “I want a big band chart and I want it in the key of F because the singer sings it that way, and I want you to modulate halfway through for a tenor solo.” They tell you exactly what you want, you don’t have to work, it’s done. But when they say, you know I got a grant one time and I
could write anything I want. Total freedom. What do you do? There was no directive. So that’s the hardest. That’s really the hard part.
Too many choices, exactly. Give me some restrictions. Give me a stop sign, give me a caution light, give me something.
